AlertSensorReadings compares a reading with configured low/high thresholds and logs normal versus critical/out-of-range results.
SensorStationOptions is a source-generated options validator target and exposes a configuration section name and polling interval.
PollingInterval is validated with TimeSpan range and HH:mm:ss regular-expression constraints.
The Sensors dictionary is required and maps station names to ThresholdOptions.
ThresholdOptions validates the required low threshold and its allowed numeric range.
ThresholdOptions validates the required high threshold and its allowed numeric range.
appsettings SensorOptions example with PollingInterval and named Roof, Roof 2, Garage and other sensor thresholds.
Continuation of the named sensor threshold configuration, including Patio.
Console output shows current sensor options and an out-of-range Garage reading.
Runtime log demonstrates normal readings, a critical Garage reading, and graceful host shutdown.
Runtime output demonstrates configuration reload: polling interval and threshold ranges change without restarting the service.
Monitoring limitations: only reload-capable providers notify changes; file shares/containers can make notifications unreliable and polling watcher may be needed.
Sensor monitor scenario: a BackgroundService reads temperature, compares options-driven thresholds, logs or alerts, waits and repeats.
OptionsMonitor.OnChange returns IDisposable; disposing the subscription unsubscribes the listener.
IOptionsMonitor provides CurrentValue for each cycle and OnChange callbacks for immediate reactions.
Reload flow: configuration provider reloads, options are rebound, CurrentValue updates and OnChange fires; intended for long-running services.
Operational gotchas for cookie ticket storage: ticket expiry, sliding expiration and Data Protection key rotation.
IPostConfigureOptions implementation assigns an injected ticket store to CookieAuthenticationOptions.SessionStore for the matching scheme.
PostConfigureCookieTicketStore helper class stores scheme and ITicketStore dependencies and implements named post-configuration.
Correct DI registration avoids BuildServiceProvider: register ticket store and construct IPostConfigureOptions from the real service provider.
IConfigureOptions runs normal configuration; IPostConfigureOptions runs afterward to finalize the options instance.
Options factory pipeline: create options, run matching configure actions, run post-configure actions, then return final options.
services.PostConfigure registers an IPostConfigureOptions action; example finalizes cookie sliding expiration and lifetime.
Named options matter for authentication schemes; post-configuration is commonly used for auth handlers, defaults, compatibility patches and validation.
Options-pattern participants: IOptions, IOptionsSnapshot, IOptionsMonitor, Configure and PostConfigure.
Why PostConfigure is preferable to BuildServiceProvider: avoid a second DI container and use constructor injection in a post-configurer.
Registration example using a real ITicketStore and PostConfigure/implementation class for CookieAuthenticationOptions.
Any options type can participate in post-configuration through IPostConfigureOptions<TOptions>.
Examples of built-in options types that can be post-configured: cookie, JWT bearer, authorization, CORS, MVC, Kestrel, forwarded headers, HTTP, antiforgery, session, JSON and custom options.
Cookie authentication is a named-options scenario created by AddAuthentication().AddCookie("Cookies", ...).
The cookie handler resolves IOptionsMonitor<CookieAuthenticationOptions>.Get("Cookies"); named Configure/PostConfigure actions participate in that pipeline.
AddCookie plus AddOptions<CookieAuthenticationOptions>("Cookies").Configure<ITicketStore> injects a service into inline configuration.
DI-aware Configure overloads resolve ITicketStore and invoke the delegate; IPostConfigureOptions is not required merely to access DI.
Conceptual behavior of a DI-aware configure overload: resolve dependency then execute configureAction(options, dependency).
OptionsBuilder exposes Configure<TDep> and multi-dependency overloads specifically for DI-aware options configuration.
PostConfigure differs mainly by ordering: it runs after normal Configure actions; both stages can be DI-aware.
AddCookie and later AddOptions configuration contribute to the same named CookieAuthenticationOptions instance rather than replacing the whole object.
Combined example: AddCookie sets name/lifetime and named PostConfigure sets SessionStore on the same options instance.
Configuration steps combine when they set different properties; for the same property, the later action wins.
AddOptions is convenient for named authentication options and provides an explicit fluent options-builder API.
Named AddOptions clearly selects the options type, name and post-configuration stage.
services.Configure<TOptions>(name, ...) and PostConfigure overloads also support named options; AddOptions is not the only route.
Why use AddOptions: fluent naming, DI-aware generic overloads and a cohesive builder chain.
Plain services.Configure/PostConfigure overloads normally accept delegates over TOptions, not the inline DI-aware delegate form.
Recommended inline DI-aware pattern for assigning ITicketStore to SessionStore through OptionsBuilder.Configure<ITicketStore>.
Precise alternatives: use AddOptions for inline DI-aware configuration, or inject dependencies into IConfigureOptions/IPostConfigureOptions classes.
Interface selection: IConfigureOptions for normal/default configuration, IPostConfigureOptions for finalization, IConfigureNamedOptions for named instances.
Example normal and post-configure classes for MyOptions, including a final minimum timeout safeguard.
IConfigureNamedOptions configures the same options type differently by name; Snapshot/Monitor can resolve names through Get(name).
MyOptions and MyNamedOptionsSetup example implementing IConfigureNamedOptions<MyOptions>.
Named Configure method applies Primary/Secondary endpoints and timeouts, while Configure(options) handles the default unnamed instance.
